Sodas and chips are displayed at a convenience store in New York City. A new lawsuit targets restrictions on sugary drinks and foods for food stamp recipients across 18 states (Shalina Chatlani/Stateline).
A lawsuit filed Wednesday seeks to block more states from restricting what kind of items food stamp recipients can buy.
Led by the National Center for Law and Economic Justice, the class action lawsuit seeks to strike down restrictions on products such as candy and soda in 18 states for recipients of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP.
It targets Arkansas, Florida, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nevada, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas, Utah, Virginia and Wyoming.
In previous litigation, a judge already blocked state and federal efforts to use waivers to restrict SNAP purchases in Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee and West Virginia.
“These unlawful waivers serve as a backdoor method to restrict access to SNAP,” Katharine Deabler-Meadows, senior attorney at the national center, said in a Wednesday news release. “Our lawsuit seeks to hold the Trump administration accountable for violating the law and causing unprecedented chaos for SNAP recipients and retailers alike.”
The Trump administration has encouraged states to seek federal waivers restricting what kinds of purchases can be made with SNAP, which has traditionally allowed recipients broad autonomy to select their own groceries.
Those waivers have targeted a variety of products but generally focus on sugary beverages and candies.
Hawaii’s waiver restricts only the purchases of soft drinks, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. But Florida’s waiver restricts purchases of soda, energy drinks, candy and prepared desserts.
The federal government argues those restrictions divert taxpayer dollars away from food purchases that fuel the nation’s epidemics of diabetes and other chronic diseases.
“These waivers help put real food back at the center of the program and empower states to lead the charge in protecting public health,” U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a statement last year.
Critics say the changes could harm people in food deserts, where healthy options are limited, and take away recipients’ power to make their own food choices. In the lawsuit, plaintiffs argue that the changes have harmed their health.
One Idaho plaintiff said she had multiple chronic health conditions including autoimmune conditions that make it difficult for her to regulate her blood pressure, heart rate and blood sugar levels. She relies on electrolyte-infused drinks and easy-to-eat foods, such as nutrition and granola bars that are now restricted in Idaho.

Another plaintiff in Oklahoma said she relied on easy-to-prepare foods as she lives in an extended-stay hotel without a kitchen. Cardinals Box Up Thanksgiving Meals for Military Veterans
Hundreds of military families in Missouri and Illinois will be receiving Thanksgiving meal kits next week, thanks to a partnership between the Cardinals and the St. Louis Area Foodbank.
A couple of dozen Cardinal employees spent their Wednesday morning packing 625 boxes with green beans, corn, apple sauce, stuffing, and macaroni and cheese. Each box is intended to feed a family of four (2,500 people total), and will also include one more side dish – a note of gratitude handwritten by someone in the Cardinals front office.
"We wanted to give back and do something for Thanksgiving to show that we really appreciate the sacrifices our veterans and military have made for our community," said Meghan Essman, director of Community Relations & Cardinals Care. "So we reached out to the food bank because they've been a great partner over the years, and they helped us put together these Thanksgiving meal packs and also bring them to Busch Stadium so that we were able to mobilize our front office."
The Cardinals donated more than $5,000 to pay for the supplies. The food bank will distribute the boxes, along with some Cardinals promotional items, to their VA partners so that military veterans and their families can enjoy a nice Thanksgiving meal.
"Being able to partner with the St. Louis Cardinals, which is such a historic organization, to give back to not only the community but to veterans specifically, just means the world to us," said Jordan Casey, Product Sourcing Project Manager for the St. Louis Area Foodbank as Cardinals employees manned three long tables and quickly assembled and stacked the boxes. "The support, getting the employees to come out like this, is inspiring. And it will kind of be a surprise to our VA partners that they’ll be receiving these Thanksgiving boxes."
The process was expected to take four hours, but Cardinals volunteers came out in such abundance that it was finished in half that time.
The St. Louis Area Foodbank covers 26 counties in Missouri and Illinois, and there is a tremendous need for its services, Casey noted, adding: "In those counties, there are enough people facing food insecurity to fill Busch Stadium 10 times."
November is a perfect time for those wishing to donate to the food bank. This month, all monetary contributions are being doubled, up to $300,000, thanks to a pledge from Ameren, Casey said.

ExxonMobil (XOM) Just Achieved Something 95% of S&P 500 (GSPC) Members Haven't Done
ExxonMobil's relatively small dividend increase was actually a big achievement.
By Selena Maranjian –
Key Points
- ExxonMobil's stock recently yielded 2.6%.
- That payout is very likely to grow over time.
In late October, the energy giant ExxonMobil (XOM -3.96%) declared a fourth-quarter dividend of $1.07 per share, payable on Dec. 10, 2026, to shareholders who owned their shares at the close of business on Nov. 16, 2026. That represented a 3.9% increase over the previous quarterly dividend of $1.03.
Ho hum, right? That information isn't remarkable -- but this is: The increase was the 44th consecutive annual dividend increase -- a feat that 95% of the companies in the S&P 500 index have not yet managed.
Companies don't usually initiate regular dividend payments until they have grown to a point where they have sufficient reliable income with which to do so. They don't want to have to reduce or suspend their dividends if they fall on hard times, because that will reflect poorly on the company and can cause shareholders and others to lose confidence. Still, even well-known and well-respected companies have had to pull back on their dividends -- such as the 50% cut in 2025 from Dow, a company founded way back in 1897.

That time period included the stock market crash in 1987, the dot-com bubble bursting in 2000, the global financial crisis in 2008, and the COVID-19 economic disruption that began in 2020, among many other events.
If you're wondering whether you should invest in ExxonMobil now, you might certainly consider doing so. Its dividend recently yielded 2.6%, and it's likely to keep growing every year, as a company with a 44-year streak is not going to want to lose that. (Once it hits 50 years, it will attain the elite rank of "Dividend King.")
Despite being near record highs, the shares seem reasonably valued at recent levels, with a forward-looking price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 13.7, a bit above the five-year average of 12.1. If you plan to hang on for many years, buying now could reward you.

Stock Market Correction: 1 Investing Move I'm Avoiding Right Now
I believe AI poses a significant market risk, but I'm not selling my technology stocks.
By Reuben Gregg Brewer –
Key Points
- I vividly remember the dot-com bubble and its aftermath.
- I bought IBM and Texas Instruments before the AI bubble got underway.
- I'm not changing my investment approach because I'm concerned that there's a market correction on the way.
The number one thing I don't want to do, at any time and for any reason, is change my long-term investment approach to fit the current market zeitgeist. It is hard to stick to a long-term plan, especially when you believe there's a material risk of a stock market correction. But history shows that while corrections come and go, the market has always resumed its upward march.
This is why, despite my concerns about an artificial intelligence (AI) bubble, I'm not selling either of my two technology stocks: International Business Machines (IBM -1.11%) and Texas Instruments (TXN -1.16%). Here's a deeper dive into why sticking to my dividend-centric investment approach trumps the risk of the AI bubble bursting.
There will be a bear market
I don't know when it will arrive, but I know with 100% certainty that there will be another bear market. And if history is any guide, a bull market will follow, eventually pushing the market to new all-time highs. That's what history shows, and you just have to look at a graph of the S&P 500 index (^GSPC -0.23%) to prove to yourself that buying and holding is a pretty good investment plan.
That said, I am a dividend investor with a value focus. My preference is to buy companies with long histories of dividend growth when they have historically high yields. I believe those two facts indicate a good business and an attractive valuation. That's how I came across IBM and Texas Instruments. At this point, IBM's dividend streak is up to 31 years, while Texas Instruments' is at 23 years.
I bought both stocks before the artificial intelligence trade took off, so my decision to jump aboard had nothing to do with that technology. I like IBM because it has an over 100-year history of adapting to the world around it, with a focus on serving business customers. I'm fond of Texas Instruments because it makes boring computer chips that go into just about every electronic device. I would fully expect the two companies to be involved in AI and, in fact, I would be upset if they didn't attempt to benefit from this still-emerging technology in some way.
I'm not getting rid of a good business
To be honest, I'd expect most of the companies I own to find a way to benefit from AI, even if that just meant using it to better serve customers or lower operating costs. But I lived through the dot-com bubble and see similarities to what is going on today with AI, which I believe is in its own bubble. If history rhymes, the bursting of the AI bubble could take the broader market down with it. The truth is, I don't just expect a stock market correction; I expect a prolonged and painful bear market led by the technology sector.

he Trump administration is launching a new effort to combat a surge in crypto fraud and other cybercrimes targeting Americans, attacks that largely come from criminal networks located overseas.
The newly formed Threat Disruption Center will operate as a technology resource and collaboration hub for the Homeland Security Task Force, the administration said Wednesday. The center, which is comprised of more than 30 federal agencies and more than 440 state and local partners, will provide tools to address complaints from scam victims and map the networks behind the criminal operations.
The effort is being established pursuant to an executive order Trump issued in March that directed government agencies to develop a response to cybercrime and fraud that are “draining American families of their life savings, stealing the benefits of years of work and destroying the lives of our youth.”
The center will “identify victims, trace victim funds back to bad actors, identify the crypto wallets utilized both by those bad actors, and then ultimately try to identify other victims,” said Eric Weindorf, deputy director of the Homeland Security Task Force’s National Coordination Center.
As part of the new effort, the government is paying TRM Labs Inc. about $95 million to provide technical support, including an artificial intelligence platform that will serve as its primary investigative tool. More than 60 TRM employees are working on the project.
“We’re looking at how can we use AI to triage victim reports in more near real time and surface opportunities where very quick action on behalf of the government could return funds to victims,” said Esteban Castaño, chief executive of TRM.
Victims in the US and abroad told the Federal Bureau of Investigation that they lost almost $21 billion to cybercrime last year, a roughly 25% surge from the previous year. Crypto-related losses accounted for more than half of that total.
The surge in fraud has posed a challenge to local law enforcement officials, in part because much of it originates overseas. It is also nearly impossible to retrieve stolen funds, which are often converted into cryptocurrency such as Bitcoin or Tether.
An outlier is the Brooklyn District Attorney’s office, which three years ago established the Virtual Currency Unit to respond to an onslaught of fraud. Run by assistant district attorney Alona Katz, the unit recently seized and disrupted more than 240 crypto-fraud websites and 112 computer servers controlled by an Eastern European fraud group, which the Brooklyn DA’s office said was “one of the biggest operational cyber disruptions undertaken by a local prosecutors’ office.”
“The Brooklyn DAs office is one of the country’s pioneers in going after these threats,” Castaño said. The Threat Disruption Center will apply the approach “across the federal government,” he said.
The government awarded the one-year agreement to TRM in July without putting it up for competitive bidding. One of TRM’s rivals, Chainalysis, sued the Trump administration, alleging that the contract awarding process was “arbitrary, capricious and unreasonable.” The lawsuit was dismissed in September.

The longest bill pays the most, and it pays more than some of the best-known dividend stocks. For a saver at or near retirement, the real question is whether a stock’s payout is worth giving up a rate the government promises to pay.
How a Treasury Bill Pays You and When Its Rate Resets
A Treasury bill is a loan to the U.S. government maturing in one year or less. You buy it for less than its face value, and when it matures, the Treasury pays you the full face value. The difference is your interest. Bills have no coupon and send you nothing along the way. According to the IRS, bills generally have a 4-, 8-, 13-, 26-, or 52-week maturity period and are issued at a discount in $100 increments.
The rate is set at auction on the day you buy. Hold the bill to maturity, and its income is fixed. When it matures, you get cash back, and to keep earning you have to roll into a new bill at whatever rate the market sets on that day. The 4.59% figure is really just a snapshot.
It goes only to bills bought at that rate. Someone rolling 4-week bills gets a new rate 13 times a year, and someone rolling 52-week bills gets one once a year. The figure stays locked for neither.
Bills carry three risks that savers often miss:
- Reinvestment risk. If rates fall, every rollover pays less. Income that looked steady can shrink quickly.
- Price risk. You can sell a bill through a broker before it matures, but if rates have risen since you bought it, you may get back less than you paid. Holding to maturity avoids this.
- Inflation risk. The face value is a fixed dollar amount, so rising prices eat into what it buys.
The government’s backing has limits too. The full faith and credit of the United States backs repayment of face value at maturity. The guarantee leaves out the price you’d get selling early, the rate on your next rollover, or what inflation does to your buying power. Bills also pay no monthly income. Getting regular checks in retirement requires staggering several maturities.
Dividend Safety Matters More Than Dividend Size
Each investment has a weakness the other lacks. A dividend can be cut. The board decides on each payment and can lower or suspend it at any time. A Treasury bill’s payout is a legal obligation fixed when you buy. A dividend can grow. A board can raise it year after year. A bill’s income changes only when rates change, and then only when you roll over. That makes dividend safety the starting point for any comparison, ahead of yield.

Today’s big story: Could Anthropic Stock Fall 25%?
Most investors expect a Fed rate hike to be good news for big banks like JPMorgan Chase. Higher rates let a bank charge more on its loans. On our data, that still holds for the business. It does not hold for the stock.
The short answer is no. Over 21 Fed hikes since June 2006, a fund of big financial stocks beat the S&P 500 in the next three months only 6 times. JPMorgan beat it after 8 of them. Since the latest hike, JPMorgan has lagged the S&P 500 so far, while that fund has beaten it.
How have bank stocks done since the September hike?
The Fed’s rise in the top of its target range to 4.0% took effect on Sept 17, 2026. It was its first increase since the one that took effect on July 27, 2023. From the close the day before through Wednesday’s close, JPMorgan returned -6.6%, counting dividends. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF, called SPY, returned -2.9%.
Two other big banks did worse. Bank of America returned -15.5% and Citigroup -11.3%. Wells Fargo returned -6.5%, about the same as JPMorgan. Our data shows no single confirmed cause for these drops.
JPMorgan has lost 6.6%, counting dividends, since the Fed hike that many owners expected to help it. If JPMorgan is a big part of your savings, that is a fall you have had to sit through. When the market has fallen, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has lost about 81 cents for every $1 its benchmark lost, on average. See the HQ record.
Did bank stocks ever rise and fall with rates?
They did, day to day. We measured how closely each stock’s daily move tracked the daily change in the 2-year Treasury yield. That yield follows where traders expect Fed rates to go. The measure is called correlation. A high positive score means the two moved together, and a score near zero means no link.
From 2016 to 2019, the yearly score of the Financial Select Sector SPDR fund (XLF) averaged 0.52. JPMorgan’s averaged 0.51. In 2026 so far, XLF’s score is -0.09 and JPMorgan’s is -0.04. The SPDR S&P Regional Banking ETF (KRE), a fund of smaller banks, is at -0.19.
Put simply, bank stocks no longer rise on days when rate expectations rise. SPY now has a negative score too, at -0.13. We think higher yields are trading as bad news for stocks in general.

Illicit Gardens cultivation facility in Kansas City (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).
Missouri cannabis regulators are asking prospective marijuana research license applicants what they want to study and what obstacles might stand in their way.
The new rules allowing marijuana research in the state go into effect Nov. 30. Ahead of that date, the Missouri Division of Cannabis Regulation is gathering feedback through an online survey “to better understand the interests, needs, and readiness of prospective applicants.”
The survey asks what kinds of studies applicants are considering, what could prevent them from obtaining or using a license and how prepared they are to begin operating.
The new rules leave the door open for many research possibilities, Amy Moore, the division’s director, said earlier this year.
“We’re all very interested in any research on cannabis and safety or its impact on the human body,” Moore said. “Certainly as a public health agency, we’re interested in health research, but it’s not limited to that. So it’ll be interesting to see what people want to propose once we get this established.”
When voters approved recreational marijuana in 2022, the constitutional amendment allowed the state to establish licenses to “facilitate scientific research or education.” But the state first had to adopt regulations. The division released draft rules last year for informal public feedback.
In May, the division asked for another round of public feedback, and the comments and the state’s responses were published in the Missouri Register in October.
A common theme among the comments was whether the state would allow seeds and clones developed through research to help licensed cultivators improve their products.
The division clarified that research licensees can sell or transfer seeds and clones developed through an approved research study to licensed cultivation facilities. Any such sale or transfer must be part of a study approved by the division.
However, marijuana sold to consumers must be grown in a licensed cultivation facility.
“Marijuana grown under experimental research conditions may pose a public health and safety risk,” the division’s response states. “Allowing the transfer of seeds and clones to cultivation facilities allows cultivation facilities to grow and cultivate marijuana plants as required in rule and in a manner that is required to meet specific testing requirements for consumer safety.”
State cannabis law requires all marijuana products sold in Missouri to originate from marijuana grown and cultivated in a Missouri-licensed facility.
The final rule states marijuana cultivation licensees have “the authority to acquire marijuana seeds and clones from a research facility if indicated within a department-approved research study.”

Emma Grace Hurley, Weini Kelati, and Jess McClain already had plenty to celebrate after earning the United States its first women's team medal at September's World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen. But nearly two months after finishing with silver, the American trio could soon have gold added to their résumés.
On Thursday, November 19, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) announced that Kenya's Veronica Loleo had received a three-year doping ban after testing positive for erythropoietin (EPO), a prohibited substance. The decision officially disqualifies her second-place finish at the September 20 event, where her silver medal helped Kenya secure the women's team title. But with Loleo's result now thrown out, Kenya's team score has to be recalculated. Countries are ranked by the combined finishing times of their three fastest athletes, and Loleo’s removal means Kenya must now count Lilian Kasait Rengeruk, who finished 34th in 1:10:36, potentially lifting the U.S. to first place in the team standings.
The Kenyan women originally led with a combined 3:17:33, ahead of the Americans' 3:19:51. But removing Loleo's 1:06:05 pushes Kenya's total to 3:22:04, leaving the U.S. in first place by two minutes and 13 seconds. Kenya would drop to second and Ethiopia would remain third, although World Athletics has yet to officially confirm the updated results.
Hurley recently acknowledged the uncertainty in a comment on Citius Mag's Instagram, noting that nobody can know exactly how the race would've unfolded without Loleo. Still, she admitted, "it would've been so cool to celebrate gold 🥹."
Loleo's sample was collected during an out-of-competition test on September 6 ahead of the championships, two weeks prior to the competition. She initially told investigators she couldn't explain the positive result, mentioning an injection she'd received for an injury, but later admitted to the violation on October 30, which earned her a one-year reduction from the standard four-year suspension.
Loleo wasn't the only major Kenyan distance runner to receive a final decision Thursday. Peres Jepchirchir, the reigning world marathon champion and 2021 Olympic gold medalist, was also handed a three-year ban following an EPO finding.
“The Kenyan authorities have made a lot of progress in the fight against doping in the last five years, but these cases highlight that there is still a long way to go,” AIU chief executive Brett Clothier said in a statement.
“The Kenyan government is aware of the current situation and has committed to further strengthen the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya and take action to address the criminal networks that facilitate doping within the country.”
Jepchirchir, who had been provisionally suspended in October, has accepted the disqualification of her results dating back to July 17, including her August victory at the Sydney Marathon. Fellow Kenyan Irine Cheptai is expected to inherit that title.

What a Price Target Really Means
A price target is an analyst's estimate of where a stock should trade in about 12 months, built from forecasts for earnings, growth and a reasonable valuation multiple. Upside is simply the gap between today's share price and the average of those targets, expressed as a percentage. Because targets are opinions rather than guarantees, they can move quickly after a company reports, and a cut does not always mean the analyst has turned negative. Sometimes a firm trims its target to reflect a stock that has already risen, or an expectations bar that was set too high, while keeping a positive rating.
That is why the rating and the target are best read together. An upgrade with a lower target tells a different story from a reiterated rating with a higher one. The reasons behind a change, such as delayed contracts, better cost control or a pricing shift, usually say more than the number does. Ranking by average upside adds a second layer. A large gap to the average target can point to a stock that has fallen out of favor as easily as to one analysts expect to take off. When a fund has an uncertain lifespan
Alternative investment funds often have a fixed lifespan. They spend the first few years buying illiquid assets and then spend the remaining years selling them off.
However, fund liabilities can have a long, uncertain lifespan, making their wind-down difficult and slow. Contingent tax liabilities can have a long tail of six or more years due to statutes of limitations in certain US jurisdictions.
Hedge funds can often give investors their money back regularly because they hold assets that are easy to sell based on investor demand for capital. But private equity funds, credit funds, infrastructure funds and real estate funds generally consist of illiquid assets that need to be sold opportunistically and generally can’t provide investors with full liquidity.
As a result, private equity fund managers will frequently advertise an expected investment period and expected fund lifespan – without making any assurances. But investors can be reluctant to invest without an indication of when they’ll see a return on their money.
Fund managers earn performance bonuses (carried interest) based on how quickly they return cash to investors. To hit these targets and wrap up an aging fund, managers sometimes sell their remaining assets to a new, secondary fund, often called a continuation fund backed by a different group of investors or a subset of the original investors.
However, fund managers struggle to control how long a fund’s financial obligations last, and buyers who take over existing funds usually don’t want to inherit old debts and risks. In the investment world, tax liabilities are especially problematic because they can linger for a very long time.
Tax liabilities, a long-tail risk
Certain tax liabilities can, of course, be eliminated by paying the appropriate tax authority. But contingent tax risks relating to uncertain positions taken by the fund can have a significantly longer tail.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration unveiled a final rule on Thursday that will make it easier for companies in some industries to classify workers as independent contractors rather than their employees, who have more legal protections and can cost more.
The Department of Labor scrapped a rule adopted during the administration of former President Joe Biden, and replaced it with a legal test favored by business groups.
The new rule could lower costs for companies in a range of industries, including trucking, healthcare, retail sales and app-based transportation and delivery services such as Uber, that rely heavily on contractors. Such companies routinely face lawsuits accusing them of misclassifying workers to save money, which they deny.
The Labor Department said the 2024 rule was legally flawed and that the new test creates a clearer standard for businesses and workers to follow.
“It’s more important than ever to ensure our labor regulations keep pace with the changing ways that Americans choose to work, and businesses choose to operate,” Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said in a statement.
The rule will take effect in January, 60 days after it is formally published.
New Rule Focuses on Control
The Biden-era rule had established factors for determining whether a worker should be classified as an employee or contractor under federal wage law, and any one of them could tip the scales toward employee status.
The rule finalized on Thursday instead focuses on whether workers are under a company’s control or have the opportunity for profit or loss based on their own initiative or investment.
Employees can cost businesses up to 30% more, according to several surveys, because they are entitled to the minimum wage, overtime pay, unemployment insurance, reimbursements for expenses and other protections not afforded to contractors.
Worker classification has been one of the most contentious employment-related issues over the last decade, and trade groups lobbied heavily to repeal the 2024 rule after an effort by Republicans in Congress to block it stalled.
The Biden-era rule had replaced a regulation adopted during Trump’s first term that said workers who own their own businesses or can work for competing companies — such as a driver who works for Uber and Lyft — can be treated as contractors. The new rule is similar to that standard.

Vaughan has 40 years of marine insurance experience spanning underwriting, reinsurance, broking and program development in the U.S., London and Bermuda markets. Most recently, Vaughan was a founding partner of Theta Special Risk, an insurance consulting and advisory firm focused on bringing technology and more efficient digital processes to the insurance industry. He previously served as a partner at McGill & Partners, where his responsibilities included MGA and reinsurance broking and the development of new programs and clients.
Earlier in his career, Vaughan co-founded specialty marine MGA Tidal Solutions and held senior marine insurance and reinsurance positions with The Chartfield Group, Quanta Capital Holdings, Willis Group, Guy Carpenter and C.T. Bowring. He began his insurance career in the London market with J.H. Minet.

Cornell University will launch a sweeping review of its Greek system and its future on campus after a report of a gang rape at a fraternity house in 2024, the university’s president said Monday.
The review will focus on the Greek system’s relationship to housing and residential life, President Michael Kotlikoff said in a letter to the Cornell community. Details will be announced in the coming weeks, he said.
The announcement marks the university’s latest response to outrage over its handling of a woman’s report that she was drugged and sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house. The woman, identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, sued Cornell and seven men in September.
Cornell expelled or suspended several students after an internal investigation and barred the fraternity chapter from campus. The accused men have denied wrongdoing, and none has been criminally charged.
Criticism of President
Kotlikoff has faced criticism for his handling of the case, including his acknowledgment that he never read the campus police report and did not follow up on the outcome of the investigations. He has defended the university’s disciplinary process and said administrators were prohibited from interfering in criminal investigations.
Cornell previously suspended parties at fraternities and announced additional measures to prevent sexual violence on campus.
“To prevent sexual assault, we must reshape the social environments, interactions, and physical spaces that can contribute to increased risk,” Kotlikoff wrote Monday.
He also outlined plans to expand sexual assault prevention education, create more late-night social opportunities outside residential spaces and establish an academic center dedicated to researching campus sexual violence. The university said it is exploring ways to revitalize businesses and develop public gathering places in Collegetown, a neighborhood near campus where many students live and socialize.
Jane Doe’s lawyers, Thomas Giuffra and Whitney Seals, said in a statement that while they welcomed action by Cornell’s administrators to address sexual assault on campus, “words, task forces, and prospective reviews cannot erase years of institutional inaction.”
“Jane Doe welcomes any genuine effort that prevents another student from enduring what she suffered. However, meaningful reform requires full transparency into how past reports of sexual violence were mishandled, real consequences for those responsible, and a permanent end to a culture that prioritizes institutional reputation over student safety,” they said.
Faculty Vote
The announcement comes just over a week after Cornell’s Faculty Senate passed a vote of no confidence in the university administration’s ability to address sexual assault on campus.
In his letter Monday, Kotlikoff directly acknowledged the loss of confidence in Cornell’s administration.

Touring the world’s largest wildlife crossing, Beth Pratt stepped carefully through freshly planted native vegetation and held up her hand for silence.
“Hear that? We’re listening to birdsong right now, on top of one of the busiest freeways in the U.S.!” a beaming Pratt, one of the project’s leaders, said excitedly. “That makes my heart glad.”
The warbling was the latest sign that the bridge, spanning U.S. 101 and a feeder road about 35 miles (56 kilometers) northwest of downtown Los Angeles, is already in use by animals ahead of the official Dec. 2 opening ceremony.
Just two weeks earlier, motion-sensor cameras captured a lone coyote believed to be the first mammal to make the trek safely across. Days after that momentous crossing, three juvenile coyotes were seen on camera playing in the brush beneath the 10-foot (3-meter) sound-dampening walls that line the span.
“They don’t care about ribbon cuttings,” laughed Pratt, president of the nonprofit Wildlife Crossing Fund.
About 300,000 cars a day travel that stretch of the 101 in Agoura Hills, a small city surrounded by a patchwork of protected wildland that the new crossing will connect. Fencing along the freeway funnels animals to the crossing.
The bridge, with a landscape that’s indistinguishable from surrounding hillsides, stretches 1,250 feet (380 meters) in two sections over the roadways to give animals hemmed in by urban sprawl a safe path to the nearby Santa Monica Mountains and beyond.
It is named the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing for the late philanthropist whose foundation donated $25 million toward the $114 million total budget. The cost ballooned from an initial $92 million, and the money came from donations from 6,000 members of the public, as well as grants from nonprofits and state funds set aside for conservation purposes. Leonardo DiCaprio was one of the earliest donors after a funding drive was launched a decade ago.
Waiting for Cougars
Pratt said for her the real official opening will be when a mountain lion, a species listed as threatened in California, finds its way to the overpass.
The star of the campaign to build the bridge was the cougar — known as P-22 — an LA celebrity in its own right who traveled across freeways and made a home in a huge Los Angeles park. P-22, who was euthanized in 2022 after likely being hit by a car, became a symbol of the shrinking genetic diversity of wild animals that must remain all but trapped by sprawling development or risk becoming roadkill. Thousands attended a memorial service for him.
Scientists tracking mountain lions fitted with GPS collars found over decades that roadways were largely confining animals in mountains that run along the Malibu coast and across the middle of Los Angeles to Griffith Park, where P-22 settled.
During the tour last week, Pratt wore a shirt emblazoned with an image of the beloved cougar. She hopes to eventually erect a statue of P-22 on the side of the new bridge.

The state of Arizona has opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI and other AI companies relating to the “apparent infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents,” Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said Wednesday.
A criminal investigation does not necessarily mean charges will be brought. Mayes said her office was investigating whether Arizona state law was being violated on an ongoing basis.
Related: California Consumer Watchdog Chief Says AI Firms That Violate State Rules Will Be Sued
“The state of Arizona is very worried about this, and we are looking at it from multiple angles,” Mayes told a press conference in Chicago.
Mayes declined to identify the other companies her office was investigating. She said her office had been in contact with Arizona banks, but declined to name them or give their responses.
Related: California Sues OpenAI Over AI Models’ Attacks on Hugging Face, Other Companies
A spokesperson for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The banking industry has become increasingly concerned that sophisticated AI agents could harm the banking system and the institutions trusted to hold people’s wealth. Reuters reported last month that major U.S. banks have been blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside customer accounts and making transactions.
Mayes’ comments come two days after California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI for allegedly developing a dangerous product without adequate safety procedures or oversight after reports that its AI models had carried out cyberattacks independently.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on that lawsuit, but the company has acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior and said it was reinforcing its safeguards. On September 16, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side of transparency “even when significance is uncertain.”
